node.label: Laurentian & national tradition
node.period_rationale: period_0, 'Earlier roots & interwar initiatives': the tradition's founding works are interwar (Mackintosh 1923, Innis 1930, Creighton 1937), and its cited core in 2009–2026 PhDs runs from Innis 1930 to Berger 1986 (median 1969). Postwar consolidation (Lower 1946, Careless 1954, the Centenary Series from 1964) follows within the main period. Chosen as for Annales and the US Progressives; not an end date.
node.date_label: Staple studies 1923–40 · Creighton 1937 · Lower 1946 · Careless 1954 · Centenary Series volumes 1964–85 · Berger's analysis 1976 · coverage through 2000

date_span.basis: Selected publication milestones only. 1923 is an early economic interpretation, not the tradition's origin; the tradition has no end date, and its works remain in use (Fur Trade cited by 49 PhDs, 2009–2026).

node.description: English-Canadian historical writing that took the transcontinental nation-state as its frame, from the interwar years to the centennial. Its economic core is the staple approach: Innis's studies of the fur trade (1930) and cod fisheries (1940) read Canada's development through exports to imperial centres, an approach Watkins later called Canada's most distinctive contribution to political economy. Creighton's Commercial Empire of the St. Lawrence (1937) simplified and expanded Innis's thesis, making Montreal's merchants the 'spiritual fathers' of Confederation; his Macdonald biography followed. Liberal nationalists such as Lower and Underhill and conservative nationalists such as Creighton and Stacey disagreed politically while sharing the nation-state as the frame of reference. Careless offered a metropolitan interpretation (1954), which Donald Davis (1985) found indeterminate, and Morton asked in 1946 on what critical premises the established interpretations rested. The Canadian Centenary Series, from 1964, gathered national syntheses, including translated volumes by the Quebec historians Trudel and Ouellet. Cook's and Careless's 'limited identities' (1967, 1969) and the new regional history of Acadiensis (1971) challenged the frame, and Berger's Writing of Canadian History (1976) analysed the English-Canadian tradition as a historiographical subject. French-Canadian historians such as Michel Brunet pursued a rival national vision, treated under Quebec historiography.
node.scope_note: A teaching umbrella, not one school. The staple approach (political economy), Creighton's Laurentian narrative, liberal and conservative nationalisms, metropolitanism and the Centenary Series are distinct projects; roster inclusion is not membership. The label avoids 'Laurentian school': no checked source uses that phrase. French-Canadian and Quebec national historiography belongs to quebec_historiography: Trudel and Ouellet are named only in the Centenary Series strand, and the Creighton–Brunet comparison is carried by the relationship note, not the roster. Stacey (official history, external policy) is placed in cdn_military and cdn_political_national; Stanley appears as a secondary row for The Birth of Western Canada. Critics appear as critics.
node.representative_figures_and_works: Mackintosh, "Economic Factors in Canadian History" (1923); Innis, The Fur Trade in Canada (1930) and The Cod Fisheries (1940); Creighton, The Commercial Empire of the St. Lawrence (1937) and John A. Macdonald (1952, 1955); Lower, Colony to Nation (1946); Underhill, In Search of Canadian Liberalism (1960); Careless, "Frontierism, Metropolitanism, and Canadian History" (1954); Morton, "Clio in Canada" (1946) and The Kingdom of Canada (1963); Canadian Centenary Series volumes by Morton (1964), Neatby (1966), Trudel (1973), Brown and Cook (1974), Ouellet (1980). Restatement: Watkins (1963). Analysis: Berger, The Writing of Canadian History (1976, 1986); Buckner (2000); Miville (2016). Critics: Cook (1967), Careless (1969), Buckner (1971), Davis (1985).

representative_people.name: W. A. Mackintosh
representative_people.context: An interwar economic interpretation of Canadian history in the CHR (1923); title-level only, not a founding claim for the staple approach.

representative_people.name: Harold A. Innis
representative_people.context: Watkins calls him "the leading innovator" of the staple approach, whose fur-trade and cod-fishery studies "stamped the 'school'"; Salmon calls The Fur Trade "for a generation the most influential English Canadian historical work". Books unread here.
representative_people.works: The Fur Trade in Canada (1930); The Cod Fisheries (1940)

representative_people.name: Donald Creighton
representative_people.context: Salmon: Creighton "simplified and expanded Innis' thesis" by making Montreal's merchants the "spiritual fathers of Confederation"; Buckner lists him as a conservative nationalist. Biographer of Macdonald. Miville compares him with Michel Brunet as a public intellectual.
representative_people.works: The Commercial Empire of the St. Lawrence (1937); John A. Macdonald (1952, 1955)

representative_people.name: A. R. M. Lower
representative_people.context: Named by Buckner (2000) as a liberal nationalist who, like conservative nationalists, took the Canadian nation-state as the frame of reference. Also wrote on the forest trade (1938).
representative_people.works: The North American Assault on the Canadian Forest (1938); Colony to Nation (1946)

representative_people.name: Frank H. Underhill
representative_people.context: A liberal nationalist in Buckner's account, quoted on Canadians' ability "to do great things together in the future". Essays unread.

representative_people.name: J. M. S. Careless
representative_people.context: A metropolitan interpretation (1954; article unread) and, in 1969, the popular statement of "limited identities" that turned the tradition toward region, culture and class (Buckner 2000). Donald Davis (1985) later questioned metropolitan theses.
representative_people.works: "Frontierism, Metropolitanism, and Canadian History" (1954); "'Limited Identities' in Canada" (1969)

representative_people.name: W. L. Morton
representative_people.context: Asked in 1946 "upon what critical premises" the established interpretations of Canadian history rested (abstract); wrote a one-volume national history and a Centenary Series volume. Primary placement proposed in cdn_regional.
representative_people.works: "Clio in Canada" (1946); The Kingdom of Canada (1963); The Critical Years (1964)

representative_people.name: George F. G. Stanley
representative_people.context: Secondary row (editorial decision, 2026-10-12), kept so that the Riel interpretation of The Birth of Western Canada (1936) is represented; it remains among the most-cited national-era works in the PhD corpus (24 PhDs, 2009–2026). Interpretation not checked here; primary placement proposed in native_newcomer.

representative_people.name: Hilda Neatby
representative_people.context: Author of the Centenary Series volume on Quebec after the Conquest (1966); catalogue level only.

representative_people.name: Robert Craig Brown
representative_people.context: Co-author of the Centenary Series volume Canada 1896–1921 (1974), the most-cited national synthesis in this set (34 PhDs, 2009–2026), and Borden's biographer.
representative_people.works: Canada 1896–1921: A Nation Transformed (1974, with Ramsay Cook)

representative_people.name: Ramsay Cook
representative_people.context: Co-author of a Centenary Series volume (1974) and, by Buckner's account, the coiner of "limited identities" (1967), which reoriented the national frame. Primary placement proposed in cdn_intellectual_cultural.

representative_people.name: Melville H. Watkins
representative_people.context: Restated the staple approach as a theory of economic growth (1963) and described it as Canada's "most distinctive contribution to political economy".

representative_people.name: Carl Berger
representative_people.context: Analyses the English-Canadian tradition in The Writing of Canadian History (1976; 2nd ed. 1986), cited by 48 PhDs (2009–2026). Book unread; its subtitle limits the subject to English-Canadian writing. Primary placement proposed in cdn_intellectual_cultural.

representative_people.name: Donald F. Davis
representative_people.context: Argues there is no single metropolitan thesis and that urban historians should abandon the metropolitan approach (1985, abstract).
representative_people.works: "The 'Metropolitan Thesis' and the Writing of Canadian Urban History" (1985)

strands.title: The staple approach
strands.focus: Development read through the export of raw materials. Watkins names Innis the innovator of a Canadian "school" whose approach was "technological history writ large" rather than growth theory; Mackintosh 1923 is an earlier economic interpretation (title only).
strands.works: W. A. Mackintosh, "Economic Factors in Canadian History," Canadian Historical Review 4, no. 1 (1923): 12–25.; Harold A. Innis, The Fur Trade in Canada: An Introduction to Canadian Economic History (New Haven: Yale University Press, 1930; rev. ed. Toronto: University of Toronto Press, 1956).; Harold A. Innis, The Cod Fisheries: The History of an International Economy (New Haven: Yale University Press; Toronto: Ryerson Press, for the Carnegie Endowment for International Peace, 1940).; A. R. M. Lower, The North American Assault on the Canadian Forest (Toronto: Ryerson Press; New Haven: Yale University Press, 1938).; Melville H. Watkins, "A Staple Theory of Economic Growth," Canadian Journal of Economics and Political Science 29, no. 2 (1963): 141–158.

strands.title: The Laurentian narrative
strands.focus: Salmon: Creighton simplified and expanded Innis by making Montreal merchants the founders of Confederation, so that politics remained the centre of the historiography. Creighton's Macdonald biography follows.
strands.works: Donald Creighton, The Commercial Empire of the St. Lawrence, 1760–1850 (Toronto: Ryerson Press; New Haven: Yale University Press, 1937); reissued as The Empire of the St. Lawrence (1956; Toronto: University of Toronto Press, 2002).; Donald Creighton, John A. Macdonald, 2 vols. (Toronto: Macmillan, 1952, 1955); vol. 2, The Old Chieftain (1955).; M. Stephen Salmon, "A Bull Market: The Recent Historiography of Canadian Economic Development," Archivaria (1997): 180–188.

strands.title: Liberal and conservative nationalists
strands.focus: Buckner (2000): Lower and Underhill (liberal) and Creighton and Stacey (conservative) differed politically while accepting the nation-state as the frame; he likens the approach to the US consensus school. Stacey is named as Buckner names him; his roster rows are in cdn_military and cdn_political_national.
strands.works: A. R. M. Lower, Colony to Nation: A History of Canada (Toronto: Longmans, Green, 1946).; Frank H. Underhill, In Search of Canadian Liberalism (Toronto: Macmillan, 1960).; P. A. Buckner, "'Limited Identities' Revisited: Regionalism and Nationalism in Canadian History," Acadiensis 30, no. 1 (Autumn 2000): 4–15.

strands.title: Metropolitanism and its critics
strands.focus: Careless's metropolitan interpretation (1954; unread) and Davis's argument (1985) that metropolitan theses are several, indeterminate about class, and best abandoned by urban historians.
strands.works: J. M. S. Careless, "Frontierism, Metropolitanism, and Canadian History," Canadian Historical Review 35, no. 1 (1954): 1–21.; Donald F. Davis, "The 'Metropolitan Thesis' and the Writing of Canadian Urban History," Urban History Review 14, no. 2 (1985): 95–113.

strands.title: Questioning the premises
strands.focus: Morton (1946) asks on what critical premises the established interpretations of Canadian history rest and what their effect has been (abstract only; the interpretations he means are not named there).
strands.works: W. L. Morton, "Clio in Canada: The Interpretation of Canadian History," University of Toronto Quarterly 15, no. 3 (1946): 227–234.; W. L. Morton, The Kingdom of Canada: A General History from Earliest Times (Toronto: McClelland and Stewart; Indianapolis: Bobbs-Merrill, 1963).

strands.title: The Canadian Centenary Series
strands.focus: A multi-volume national history (volumes 1964–85 in this draft) whose catalogue records show translated volumes by Marcel Trudel (1973) and Fernand Ouellet (1980) beside English-Canadian authors. Trudel and Ouellet are named here for those volumes only; both are placed in quebec_historiography, not on this roster. Editorial direction not checked.

strands.title: The tradition as historiography

proposed_relationships.relationship: An English-Canadian instance of national narrative
proposed_relationships.evidence_note: Buckner (2000, pp. 4–5): before the 1960s Canadian historians emphasized "the economic and political unity of Canada as it evolved from a colony into an independent nation-state", and "virtually every English-Canadian historian accepted the legitimacy of the Canadian nation-state as a frame of reference". Morton (1946) treats "well-defined interpretations of Canadian history" as objects of criticism. Comparison only: the atlas umbrella is broader and includes anticolonial counter-histories; no descent is claimed.

proposed_relationships.relationship: The staple approach as a Canadian contribution to economic history
proposed_relationships.evidence_note: Watkins (1963): the staple approach "is primarily a Canadian innovation; indeed, it is Canada's most distinctive contribution to political economy", with Innis as "the leading innovator". Salmon (1997): the staple thesis gave "an economic rationale for Canadian political development". Contribution to the field, not a claim that economic history adopted it generally. The atlas economic entry has no Canadian anchors, so no PhD overlap is computed.

proposed_relationships.relationship: National consensus in Canadian and US historiography
proposed_relationships.evidence_note: Buckner (2000, p. 5) calls the pre-1960s Canadian approach "similar to that of the consensus school in the United States": minimizing internal divisions and stressing what united Canadians. Comparison with the consensus half of the atlas entry only. Careless's 1954 title engages "frontierism", but the article is unread; no Turner influence is claimed.

Miville (2016) compares Creighton and Brunet as public intellectuals: both denounced official bilingualism, Creighton to defend Macdonald's founding vision, Brunet because the country was built by two nations. The Centenary Series translated Trudel (1973) and Ouellet (1980) into the English national synthesis; Berger's subtitle restricts his analysis to English-Canadian writing. Comparison, not influence. PhD context: 68 of 173 2009–2026 PhDs engaged with cdn_national_tradition also engage the quebec_historiography anchor set (39% vs 16% of all; lift 2.51). Bibliographies record consultation, not influence.
proposed_relationships.merge_note: Same pair and kind as qcreq_rel_04 in the quebec_historiography draft (title-level, Brunet 1958), whose drafter asked for a stronger witness. Accept one edge carrying both source sets.

proposed_relationships.relationship: Urban history rejects the metropolitan thesis
proposed_relationships.evidence_note: Davis (1985, abstract): metropolitan theses are several rather than one; their indeterminacy about relations between classes is why urban historians "feraient mieux d'abandonner complètement l'approche métropolitaine". Targets the metropolitan strand only, not the staple approach or national synthesis.
